subject: Ancient History
theme: The Gupta Empire — Rise and Fall

items.label: Chandragupta I establishes the Gupta Empire
Samudragupta's conquests recorded in the Allahabad Prashasti
Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) begins his reign
Huna invasions begin, resisted by Skandagupta
Gupta Empire effectively ends

explanation: The Guptas rose through Chandragupta I's founding marriage alliance, Samudragupta's military expansion, and Chandragupta II's golden-age patronage of arts and science — before repeated Huna invasions from the mid-5th century wore the empire down over the following century.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Mature phase of the Harappan Civilisation begins
Composition of the Rigveda
Rise of the sixteen Mahajanapadas
Chandragupta Maurya founds the Mauryan Empire
Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire

explanation: This is the backbone chronology of ancient India: urban Harappan cities, then the Vedic age, then territorial Mahajanapadas, and finally the two great pan-Indian empires — the Mauryas and, some six centuries later, the Guptas.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Chandragupta Maurya seizes the Nanda throne
Bindusara succeeds Chandragupta
Ashoka's accession to the throne
Last Mauryan king Brihadratha assassinated by Pushyamitra Shunga

explanation: The Mauryan Empire passed from its founder Chandragupta to his son Bindusara and then to Ashoka; about half a century after Ashoka's death, the dynasty ended when its commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last king in 185 BCE.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha
Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali
Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra under Ashoka
Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Kanishka

explanation: The councils track Buddhism's institutional evolution: the first compiled the Buddha's teachings just after his death, the second saw the Mahasanghika split, Ashoka's third council sent out missionaries, and Kanishka's fourth council is associated with the rise of Mahayana.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Persian (Achaemenid) campaign into the Indus region
Alexander's invasion of northwest India
Indo-Greek invasions begin
Saka rule established in western India
Kushan rule established under Kadphises

explanation: India saw a long sequence of overland invasions from the northwest, each leaving successors who eventually assimilated. The Persians came first, followed by Alexander, then Indo-Greek kings, Sakas, and finally the Kushans — who built one of ancient India's most extensive empires.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Megasthenes arrives at Chandragupta Maurya's court
Fa-Hien travels through Gupta India
Hiuen Tsang arrives in India during Harsha's reign
I-tsing studies at Nalanda

explanation: Each traveller anchors a ruler: Megasthenes came as Seleucus's envoy to Chandragupta Maurya, Fa-Hien saw Chandragupta II's Gupta realm, Hiuen Tsang was welcomed by Harsha, and I-tsing documented monastic life at Nalanda a generation later.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Bimbisara begins Haryanka rule
Shishunaga dynasty replaces the Haryankas
Mahapadma Nanda founds the Nanda dynasty
Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas
Pushyamitra Shunga founds the Shunga dynasty

explanation: Magadha's throne passed through a fixed sequence — Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda, Maurya, Shunga — with each dynasty typically ending in a coup by its own minister or general.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Taxila flourishes as a centre of learning
Nalanda Mahavihara founded under Kumaragupta I
Valabhi university flourishes under the Maitrakas
Vikramashila founded by Pala king Dharmapala

explanation: India's ancient universities rose in sequence: Taxila in the far northwest during the late Vedic age, Nalanda under Gupta patronage, Valabhi in Gujarat under the Maitrakas, and Vikramashila as the Palas' great Buddhist foundation in the east.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Harappa excavated by Daya Ram Sahni
Mohenjo-daro excavated by R. D. Banerji
Kalibangan identified by A. Ghosh
Lothal discovered by S. R. Rao
Dholavira discovered by J. P. Joshi

explanation: The civilisation itself was revealed in 1921-22 with the twin digs at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; after Partition placed both in Pakistan, Indian archaeologists located major sites at home — Kalibangan, Lothal and finally Dholavira.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Kalinga War transforms Ashoka
Major Rock Edicts issued
Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra
Pillar Edicts inscribed
Death of Ashoka

explanation: Everything follows from Kalinga: the remorseful emperor turned to dhamma, broadcast it first on rock edicts, convened the Third Council to purify the sangha, and issued the pillar edicts late in a reign that ended around 232 BCE.

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Vikram Samvat era begins
Saka era begins (linked to Kanishka's accession)
Gupta era begins with Chandragupta I
Harsha era begins with Harshavardhana's accession

explanation: Indian inscriptions date events by eras founded at royal accessions: Vikram Samvat (57 BCE), the Saka era (78 CE, later adopted as India's national calendar), the Gupta era (320 CE) and the Harsha era (606 CE).

subject: Ancient History

items.label: Alexander invades northwest India, Battle of Hydaspes
Alexander dies at Babylon
Chandragupta Maurya founds his empire
Seleucus cedes territory to Chandragupta by treaty
Bindusara succeeds Chandragupta

explanation: Alexander's withdrawal and death created a power vacuum in the northwest that Chandragupta exploited within two years; his treaty with Seleucus around 305 BCE fixed the empire's western frontier before Bindusara inherited it.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Mamluk (Slave) dynasty founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak
Khilji dynasty founded by Jalaluddin Khilji
Tughlaq dynasty founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
Sayyid dynasty founded by Khizr Khan
Lodi dynasty founded by Bahlul Lodi

explanation: Five dynasties ruled the Delhi Sultanate in unbroken sequence over roughly 250 years, ending when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 to found the Mughal Empire.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Babur becomes the first Mughal emperor
Humayun succeeds Babur
Akbar's accession at Kalanaur
Jahangir's accession
Shah Jahan's accession

explanation: The succession of the first five Great Mughals runs Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan — with Akbar's fifty-year reign (1556-1605) forming the empire's consolidating core.

subject: Medieval History
theme: Decisive Battles of the Medieval Era

items.label: First Battle of Panipat — Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi
Battle of Khanwa — Babur defeats Rana Sanga
Second Battle of Panipat — Akbar's forces defeat Hemu
Battle of Haldighati — Akbar's forces against Maharana Pratap
Third Battle of Panipat — Abdali defeats the Marathas

explanation: Panipat bookends the Mughal story: the first battle founded the empire, Khanwa secured it against the Rajputs, the second battle restored it for Akbar, and the third — fought between Afghans and Marathas — marked how completely Mughal power had hollowed out by 1761.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Vijayanagara Empire founded by Harihara and Bukka
Bahmani Sultanate founded by Alauddin Bahman Shah
Krishnadevaraya's accession
Battle of Talikota shatters Vijayanagara

explanation: The two great Deccan rivals were founded a decade apart in the mid-14th century; Vijayanagara peaked under Krishnadevaraya before the combined Deccan sultanates — successors of the Bahmani kingdom — destroyed it at Talikota in 1565.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Alauddin Khilji's accession after killing Jalaluddin
Conquest of Gujarat
Capture of Chittor
Malik Kafur's campaign reaches Madurai

explanation: Alauddin expanded in two directions: he personally led conquests in the north and west (Gujarat, Chittor) while his general Malik Kafur raided deep into the peninsula, reaching the Pandyan capital Madurai by 1311.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's accession
Capital transferred from Delhi to Daulatabad
Token copper currency introduced
Ibn Battuta arrives at his court
Muhammad bin Tughlaq dies campaigning in Sindh

explanation: His two most famous experiments — the capital shift and the token currency — came in quick succession early in the reign, and both failed. Ibn Battuta arrived in time to record the aftermath, and the sultan died in 1351 still suppressing rebellions.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Humayun's accession
Battle of Chausa — Sher Khan defeats Humayun
Battle of Kannauj — Humayun driven from India
Sher Shah dies at Kalinjar
Humayun recaptures Delhi

explanation: Sher Shah defeated Humayun twice in successive years (Chausa 1539, Kannauj 1540) and ruled an interregnum famous for administrative reform; only after Sher Shah's death and the Sur dynasty's decay could Humayun return in 1555 — dying months later.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Birth of Shivaji at Shivneri fort
Treaty of Purandar with Jai Singh
Shivaji escapes from Aurangzeb's detention at Agra
Coronation at Raigad as Chhatrapati
Death of Shivaji

explanation: The Purandar treaty and the Agra escape came back-to-back in 1665-66 — the low point of Shivaji's fortunes — after which he rebuilt his power, crowned himself Chhatrapati in 1674, and ruled a sovereign Maratha state until his death.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Birth of Ramanuja
Birth of Kabir (traditional date)
Birth of Guru Nanak
Birth of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu
Birth of Tulsidas (traditional date)

explanation: Ramanuja's 11th-century Vishishtadvaita laid the philosophical ground; the popular north Indian wave came much later, with Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya and Tulsidas all born within about a century of each other (c. 1440-1532).

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Death of Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar
Death of Bahadur Shah I
Farrukhsiyar's farman grants the East India Company trade privileges
Nadir Shah sacks Delhi and takes the Peacock Throne
Third Battle of Panipat

explanation: After Aurangzeb, weak successions came fast — Bahadur Shah I ruled only five years — while the 1717 farman quietly empowered the English Company; Nadir Shah's 1739 sack exposed imperial impotence long before Panipat III confirmed it.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Balaji Vishwanath becomes Peshwa
Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) becomes Peshwa
Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat

explanation: The Peshwaship became hereditary from Balaji Vishwanath; Baji Rao I's cavalry campaigns spread Maratha power across north India, and under Balaji Baji Rao the expansion peaked — then broke catastrophically at Panipat in 1761.

subject: Medieval History

items.label: Marco Polo visits south India
Ibn Battuta arrives at Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Delhi
Abdur Razzaq visits Vijayanagara under Deva Raya II
Athanasius Nikitin, the Russian, travels in the Bahmani Deccan
Domingo Paes describes Vijayanagara under Krishnadevaraya

explanation: Match traveller to host kingdom: Marco Polo saw the Pandyan coast, Ibn Battuta served the Tughlaqs, Abdur Razzaq was Persia's envoy to Deva Raya II, Nikitin wandered the Bahmani Deccan, and Paes recorded Vijayanagara at its Krishnadevaraya-era peak.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Champaran Satyagraha — Gandhi's first in India
Kheda Satyagraha for peasants of Gujarat
Non-Cooperation Movement launched
Civil Disobedience Movement begins with the Dandi March
Quit India Movement launched

explanation: Gandhi scaled up in stages — local satyagrahas at Champaran and Kheda proved the method, then three nationwide waves followed roughly a decade apart: Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930) and Quit India (1942).

subject: Modern History

items.label: Battle of Plassey
Battle of Buxar
Fall of Srirangapatna and death of Tipu Sultan
Annexation of Punjab after the Second Anglo-Sikh War
Revolt of 1857 begins at Meerut

explanation: Company power spread outward from Bengal: Plassey and Buxar secured the east, Tipu's fall in 1799 broke southern resistance, Punjab's annexation in 1849 completed the map — and eight years later the 1857 Revolt shook the whole edifice.

subject: Modern History
theme: Milestones of the Indian National Congress

items.label: Indian National Congress founded in Bombay
Surat Split between Moderates and Extremists
Lucknow session reunites the factions and seals the pact with the Muslim League
Calcutta special session approves Non-Cooperation
Lahore session adopts Purna Swaraj
Karachi session resolution on Fundamental Rights

explanation: Congress evolved from a petitioning body into a mass movement: it split at Surat, healed at Lucknow, embraced Gandhian mass politics in 1920, declared complete independence at Lahore, and spelt out a rights-based vision at Karachi.

subject: Modern History

items.label: August Offer by Viceroy Linlithgow
Cripps Mission
Shimla Conference under Viceroy Wavell
Cabinet Mission Plan
Mountbatten Plan and Partition

explanation: Each wartime and post-war offer conceded more than the last: dominion-style promises in 1940 and 1942 failed, the Shimla and Cabinet Mission negotiations collapsed over communal representation, and Mountbatten's 1947 plan finally paired freedom with partition.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Partition of Bengal announced by Curzon
All-India Muslim League founded in Dacca
Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act)
Lucknow Pact between Congress and Muslim League
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act)

explanation: Partition of Bengal sharpened political mobilisation and helped trigger the Muslim League's founding a year later. Reform acts followed at either end of the Lucknow Pact, and the disappointment with the 1919 reforms — alongside the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh the same year — set up the 1920 Non-Cooperation Movement.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Integration of princely states begins
Operation Polo — Hyderabad annexed
States Reorganisation Act passed
Goa liberated from Portuguese rule (Operation Vijay)
Tashkent Agreement ends the Indo-Pak War

explanation: Independence in 1947 was only the start of territorial consolidation — Hyderabad was absorbed by force in 1948, states were redrawn on linguistic lines in 1956, Goa was taken from Portugal in 1961, and by 1966 India had fought and settled its second war with Pakistan.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Brahmo Samaj founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy
Prarthana Samaj founded in Bombay
Satyashodhak Samaj founded by Jyotiba Phule
Arya Samaj founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati
Ramakrishna Mission founded by Swami Vivekananda

explanation: Reform began in Bengal with the Brahmo Samaj, then spread west — Prarthana Samaj in Bombay, Phule's anti-caste Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune, Dayananda's Arya Samaj in the same decade — before Vivekananda institutionalised Ramakrishna's legacy in 1897.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Regulating Act
Pitt's India Act
Charter Act ending the Company's India trade monopoly
Charter Act making the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India
Government of India Act transfers rule to the Crown

explanation: Parliament tightened its grip on the Company step by step — first oversight (1773), then dual control (1784), then stripping trade monopolies (1813, 1833) — until the 1857 Revolt prompted the Crown to take over entirely in 1858.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Chapekar brothers assassinate Rand in Pune
Muzaffarpur bombing and the Alipore Bomb Case
Ghadar Party founded in North America
Kakori train action by the Hindustan Republican Association
Chittagong armoury raid led by Surya Sen

explanation: Revolutionary violence came in waves: the Pune assassinations of 1897, the Bengal bomb cult around 1908, the diaspora-based Ghadar network from 1913, and the HRA/HSRA generation whose Kakori and Chittagong actions bracketed the late 1920s.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Sanyasi-Fakir rebellion in Bengal
Santhal rebellion (Hul) led by Sidhu and Kanhu
Indigo revolt in Bengal
Deccan riots against moneylenders
Munda ulgulan led by Birsa Munda

explanation: Rural India resisted colonial extraction repeatedly: famine-era Sanyasi bands in the 1770s, the great Santhal Hul of 1855, indigo cultivators in 1859, indebted Deccan peasants in 1875, and Birsa Munda's millenarian ulgulan at the century's close.

subject: Modern History
theme: Civil Disobedience Years, Month by Month

items.label: Dandi March begins
First Round Table Conference opens in London
Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed
Second Round Table Conference with Gandhi attending
Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar

explanation: The sequence alternates agitation and negotiation: Dandi launched civil disobedience, Congress boycotted the first RTC, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact bought a truce so Gandhi could attend the second RTC, and after its failure the Communal Award crisis ended in the Poona Pact.

subject: Modern History

items.label: Hicky's Bengal Gazette, India's first newspaper
Sambad Kaumudi started by Raja Ram Mohan Roy
Amrita Bazar Patrika founded
Kesari launched by Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Gandhi takes over Young India

explanation: The press grew from Hicky's scandal sheet into a nationalist weapon: Ram Mohan Roy pioneered reformist journalism, Amrita Bazar Patrika and Tilak's Kesari carried the national movement, and Gandhi made Young India his own mouthpiece from 1919.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Akbar begins rebuilding Agra Fort
Humayun's Tomb completed in Delhi
Fatehpur Sikri founded as Akbar's capital
Red Fort of Shahjahanabad completed
Taj Mahal complex completed

explanation: Akbar's building spree of the 1560s-70s (Agra Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri) established the Mughal style in red sandstone; under Shah Jahan the idiom matured into white-marble grandeur at the Red Fort and the Taj.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Great Stupa at Sanchi commissioned by Ashoka
Bharhut stupa railings carved under the Shungas
Great Chaitya at Karle excavated
Ajanta murals painted under Vakataka patronage

explanation: Buddhist art moved from Ashoka's brick-and-stone stupas through Shunga-era narrative railings at Bharhut to the great western Ghats rock-cut chaityas like Karle, culminating in the painted splendour of Ajanta's Vakataka phase.

subject: Art and Culture
theme: Monuments of Sultanate and Mughal Delhi

items.label: Qutub Minar begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak
Alai Darwaza built by Alauddin Khilji
Tughlaqabad fort city founded
Bara Gumbad built in the Lodi Gardens complex
Jama Masjid of Shahjahanabad completed

explanation: Delhi's skyline records its dynasties in order: the Slave dynasty's Qutub Minar, the Khilji Alai Darwaza with its true arch, the austere Tughlaq fortress city, Lodi-era tomb architecture, and finally Shah Jahan's imperial Jama Masjid.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Asiatic Society founded by William Jones in Calcutta
Indian Museum established in Calcutta
Archaeological Survey of India founded under Alexander Cunningham
Sangeet Natak Akademi set up
Sahitya Akademi inaugurated

explanation: Colonial-era orientalist scholarship created the Asiatic Society, the Indian Museum and the ASI; after independence, the state built its own cultural apparatus, starting with the Akademis for performing arts (1952) and literature (1954).

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Kailasa Temple, Ellora, commissioned by Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
Brihadeeswarar Temple, Thanjavur, completed under Chola king Rajaraja I
Konark Sun Temple built under the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I
Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) completed, Adi Granth installed
Meenakshi Temple, Madurai, majorly expanded under Nayaka ruler Tirumalai Nayak

explanation: Temple architecture spans nearly a millennium of dynastic patronage — Rashtrakuta rock-cut work at Ellora, Chola engineering at Thanjavur, Eastern Ganga solar symbolism at Konark, Sikh Gurus at Amritsar, and Nayaka-era expansion at Madurai.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Dashavatara temple at Deogarh — early Gupta structural temple
Shore Temple at Mamallapuram under Pallava Rajasimha
Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho under the Chandellas
Chennakesava temple at Belur begun by Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana
Ramappa temple in Telangana begun under the Kakatiyas

explanation: From the simple flat-roofed Gupta shrine at Deogarh, temple building diverged into regional styles — Pallava structural Dravida at the Shore Temple, mature Nagara at Khajuraho, and the ornate star-plan idioms of the Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Ajanta cave murals painted
Pala school of palm-leaf manuscript miniatures flourishes
Mughal atelier takes shape under Akbar
Kangra school of Pahari painting at its peak
Progressive Artists' Group formed in Bombay

explanation: Indian painting runs from classical wall murals at Ajanta through Pala manuscript illumination, the Persian-influenced Mughal atelier, and lyrical Kangra miniatures, to the modernist break made by the Progressive Artists' Group in 1947.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Panini composes the Ashtadhyayi
Kautilya's Arthashastra (traditional date)
Kalidasa writes Abhijnanashakuntalam in the Gupta age
Banabhatta writes the Harshacharita
Jayadeva composes the Gita Govinda

explanation: Sanskrit's landmarks track its patrons: Panini's grammar fixed the language, the Arthashastra served Mauryan statecraft, Kalidasa adorned the Gupta court, Bana chronicled Harsha, and Jayadeva's Gita Govinda flowered under the Gangas of Odisha.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Punch-marked silver coins in circulation
Indo-Greek kings issue portrait coins
Kushan gold coinage begins under Vima Kadphises
Gupta dinaras depict kings as archers and musicians
Sher Shah Suri standardises the silver rupiya

explanation: Coinage evolved from anonymous punch-marked silver to Indo-Greek portraiture, then dynastic gold under the Kushans and artistic Gupta dinaras — and Sher Shah's 16th-century rupiya gave India the very name of its modern currency.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Dnyaneshwari composed in Marathi by Dnyaneshwar
Amuktamalyada composed in Telugu by Krishnadevaraya
Tulsidas begins the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi
Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan

explanation: Bhakti's great books are milestones of vernacular literature: Dnyaneshwar's Marathi Gita commentary in 1290, a Telugu masterpiece by an emperor around 1515, Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramayana from 1574, and the Adi Granth anthology of saint-poets in 1604.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Mesolithic paintings at Bhimbetka rock shelters
Barabar caves cut under Mauryan patronage for the Ajivikas
Ajanta's great Vakataka-phase caves excavated
Badami cave temple of Mangalesha dedicated
Kailasa temple carved at Ellora

explanation: India's rock-cut tradition begins with prehistoric painting at Bhimbetka, turns architectural with the polished Mauryan Barabar caves, and climaxes in the Deccan sequence Ajanta → Badami → Ellora, ending with a whole temple carved from a single cliff.

subject: Art and Culture

items.label: Ashokan Major Rock Edicts in Prakrit
Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman — early courtly Sanskrit
Allahabad Pillar Prashasti of Samudragupta by Harishena
Mehrauli iron pillar inscription of 'King Chandra'
Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II by Ravikirti

explanation: Inscriptions trace the shift from Ashoka's Prakrit moral edicts to Sanskrit royal eulogy — Rudradaman's Junagadh record is the first great courtly Sanskrit text, followed by the Gupta prashastis and the Chalukyan showpiece at Aihole.

subject: Geography

items.label: Gondwanaland begins to break apart
Indian plate separates and drifts northward
Deccan Trap volcanic eruptions
Indian plate collides with the Eurasian plate
Siwalik ranges form from Himalayan debris

explanation: India's physiography is a drift story: the subcontinent broke off Gondwana, erupted the Deccan lavas en route north, rammed into Eurasia to raise the Himalayas, and the youngest range — the Siwaliks — formed last from the mountains' own eroded debris.

subject: Geography

items.label: First (non-synchronous) census of India
First synchronous decennial census
'Year of the Great Divide' — population growth turns upward
First census of independent India
Latest completed census

explanation: The census began under Lord Mayo in 1872 and became a synchronised decennial exercise from 1881; 1921 is the demographic 'Great Divide' after which population rose continuously, and 2011 remains the last completed count.

subject: Geography

items.label: Damodar Valley Corporation established
Hirakud Dam on the Mahanadi completed
Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej completed
Tehri Dam on the Bhagirathi commissioned
Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada inaugurated at full height

explanation: The early multipurpose projects — DVC (modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority), Hirakud and Bhakra — were Nehru-era 'temples of modern India'; Tehri and Sardar Sarovar took decades longer amid engineering and environmental controversy.

subject: Geography
theme: The Age of Exploration and Great Canals

items.label: Columbus reaches the Americas
Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut via the Cape of Good Hope
Magellan's expedition departs to circumnavigate the globe
Suez Canal opens
Panama Canal opens

explanation: The 1490s voyages of Columbus and da Gama opened the ocean world, Magellan's fleet proved it was one connected sea, and the two great 19th-20th century canals — Suez and Panama — rewired global shipping routes.

subject: Geography

items.label: Andhra Pradesh formed as India's first linguistic state
Bombay State bifurcated into Maharashtra and Gujarat
Nagaland becomes the 16th state
Sikkim becomes a full state
Telangana carved out of Andhra Pradesh

explanation: State boundaries in independent India were redrawn in waves — first along linguistic lines following the States Reorganisation Commission, then through later bifurcations driven by regional identity movements, right up to Telangana in 2014.

subject: Geography

items.label: Survey of India established
Great Trigonometrical Survey begins under Lambton
Peak XV computed as the world's highest mountain
Peak XV officially named Mount Everest
Hillary and Tenzing make the first ascent of Everest

explanation: The Survey of India's Great Trigonometrical Survey, begun in 1802, methodically triangulated the subcontinent; its computers identified Peak XV as the world's highest in 1852, it was named for a former Surveyor-General in 1865, and was finally climbed in 1953.

subject: Geography

items.label: Durand Line drawn between British India and Afghanistan
McMahon Line drawn at the Simla Convention
Radcliffe Line partitions India and Pakistan
Line of Control established by the Simla Agreement

explanation: Each line marks a different negotiation: the colonial Durand and McMahon lines fixed frontiers with Afghanistan and Tibet, Radcliffe's hurried award drew the Partition boundary, and the 1972 Simla Agreement converted the Kashmir ceasefire line into the LoC.

subject: Geography
theme: India's River Water Agreements and Links

items.label: Indus Waters Treaty signed with Pakistan
Farakka Barrage on the Ganga commissioned
Ganga Water Sharing Treaty signed with Bangladesh
Ken-Betwa river link project approved by the Union Cabinet

explanation: India's transboundary water diplomacy began with the World Bank-brokered Indus treaty; Farakka's commissioning created the Ganga dispute that the 1996 treaty with Bangladesh settled, while Ken-Betwa launched the domestic river-interlinking era.

subject: Geography

items.label: Aryabhata, India's first satellite, launched
Bhaskara-I experimental earth observation satellite
IRS-1A, first operational remote sensing satellite
Oceansat-1 (IRS-P4) launched for ocean studies
Cartosat-1 launched for high-resolution mapping

explanation: India's remote sensing programme matured in steps: the experimental Aryabhata and Bhaskara missions led to the operational IRS series from 1988, then specialised platforms — Oceansat for the seas and Cartosat for cartographic-grade imagery.

subject: Geography

items.label: Bihar-Nepal earthquake
Latur (Killari) earthquake in Maharashtra
Bhuj earthquake in Gujarat
Indian Ocean tsunami strikes India's east coast
Kedarnath flash floods in Uttarakhand

explanation: These disasters reshaped Indian disaster policy: the Latur and Bhuj earthquakes exposed vulnerability outside the Himalayan belt, and the 2004 tsunami directly led to the Disaster Management Act of 2005 and India's tsunami warning system.

subject: Geography

items.label: First Indian Antarctic expedition
Dakshin Gangotri, first Indian Antarctic station
Maitri station commissioned
Bharati station commissioned
Indian Antarctic Act enacted

explanation: India's polar presence grew from the pioneering 1981 expedition to three successive stations — Dakshin Gangotri (later buried in ice), Maitri and Bharati — and in 2022 Parliament gave the programme a domestic legal framework.

subject: Geography

items.label: New Delhi inaugurated as the imperial capital
Bhubaneswar planned as Odisha's new capital
Chandigarh, designed by Le Corbusier, inaugurated
Foundation stone laid for Amaravati, Andhra Pradesh

explanation: Purpose-built capitals bookend Indian planning history: Lutyens' imperial New Delhi, the early post-independence projects at Bhubaneswar and Chandigarh, and the still-unfinished 21st-century experiment at Amaravati.

subject: Economy

items.label: First Five-Year Plan launched
Green Revolution begins with high-yield variety seeds
First round of bank nationalisation (14 banks)
LPG reforms — liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation
Goods and Services Tax (GST) implemented

explanation: India's economic story moves from planned self-sufficiency (Five-Year Plans, nationalised banks) through a productivity push (Green Revolution) to a decisive market opening in 1991, culminating decades later in a single unified indirect tax regime.

subject: Economy

items.label: Reserve Bank of India established
RBI nationalised
State Bank of India formed from the Imperial Bank
Fourteen major banks nationalised
Six more banks nationalised

explanation: Banking moved steadily into state hands: the RBI was created private in 1935 and nationalised in 1949, the Imperial Bank became SBI in 1955, and the big nationalisation waves of 1969 and 1980 brought most commercial banking under government ownership.

subject: Economy
theme: The Planning Era and Its End

items.label: First Five-Year Plan begins (Harrod-Domar based)
Second Plan adopts the Mahalanobis heavy-industry model
'Plan Holiday' begins after wars and drought
Twelfth (and last) Five-Year Plan begins
NITI Aayog replaces the Planning Commission

explanation: Five-Year Plans ran from 1951, with the Mahalanobis Second Plan setting the heavy-industry course and the 1966-69 Plan Holiday marking the first big break; the Twelfth Plan (2012-17) proved the last as NITI Aayog ended the era in 2015.

subject: Economy

items.label: New Economic Policy launches LPG reforms
SEBI given statutory powers
FEMA replaces the draconian FERA
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code enacted
GST rolled out nationwide

explanation: The 1991 crisis-driven opening was followed by institution building: a statutory market regulator in 1992, liberalised forex law in 1999, and the twin structural reforms of the 2010s — the bankruptcy code and the GST.

subject: Economy
theme: Evolution of Monetary Policy in India

items.label: RBI Act passed
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act
Monetary Policy Framework Agreement adopts inflation targeting
Monetary Policy Committee holds its first meeting

explanation: The RBI Act of 1934 created the central bank, but the modern framework is recent: FRBM disciplined fiscal policy in 2003, the 2015 agreement fixed a 4% CPI inflation target, and the six-member MPC began setting rates in 2016.

subject: Economy

items.label: IFCI, India's first development bank, established
ICICI set up to finance private industry
IDBI established as the apex industrial lender
NABARD created for agriculture and rural development
SIDBI created for small industries

explanation: India built specialised lenders one sector at a time: IFCI for industry in 1948, ICICI for private enterprise, IDBI as apex institution in 1964, then dedicated banks for agriculture (NABARD, 1982) and small industry (SIDBI, 1990).

subject: Economy
theme: The Long Road of Indirect Tax Reform

items.label: Income Tax Act consolidates direct taxation
MODVAT introduced to reduce cascading of excise duties
Service tax introduced on three services
State-level VAT replaces sales tax
GST subsumes central and state indirect taxes

explanation: Every step chipped away at tax cascading: MODVAT gave credit for excise inputs, service tax broadened the base from 1994, state VAT rationalised sales taxes in 2005, and GST finally merged the chain into one destination-based tax in 2017.

subject: Economy

items.label: Green Revolution begins with HYV seeds
Operation Flood launches the White Revolution
Kisan Credit Card scheme introduced
National Food Security Act enacted
PM-KISAN direct income support launched

explanation: Farm policy shifted focus over the decades — first raising production (Green and White Revolutions), then easing credit (KCC), then guaranteeing food access as a legal right (NFSA 2013), and finally direct cash transfers to farmers (PM-KISAN).

subject: Economy

items.label: Hilton Young Commission recommends creating the RBI
Narasimham Committee I on financial sector reform
Narasimham Committee II on banking sector reform
Nachiket Mor Committee on financial inclusion set up
P. J. Nayak Committee reports on bank board governance

explanation: The Hilton Young Commission fathered the RBI itself; the two Narasimham committees scripted post-1991 liberalisation of banking, while the Mor and Nayak committees of 2013-14 drove the payments-bank push and the governance debate in public sector banks.

subject: Economy

items.label: First post-independence devaluation of the rupee
Major devaluation of 1966
Two-step crisis devaluation of July 1991
LERMS introduces partial convertibility
Rupee made fully convertible on the current account

explanation: Three devaluations (1949, 1966, 1991) mark the fixed-rate era's crises; after 1991 the regime itself changed, moving through the dual-rate LERMS to a market-determined rate and full current account convertibility by 1994.

subject: Economy

items.label: Bombay Stock Exchange founded
SEBI constituted as a non-statutory body
SEBI Act gives the regulator statutory powers
NSE begins equity trading with screen-based system
NSDL launches dematerialised share holding

explanation: Asia's oldest exchange operated for over a century before modern regulation arrived: SEBI (statutory after the 1992 securities scam), the NSE's electronic trading from 1994, and NSDL's demat system in 1996 together transformed Indian markets.

subject: Economy
theme: Industrial Policy from Control to Liberalisation

items.label: Industrial Policy Resolution defines a mixed economy
Industries (Development and Regulation) Act introduces licensing
Industrial Policy Resolution reserves the commanding heights for the state
MRTP Act restricts large business houses
New Industrial Policy abolishes most licensing

explanation: Control tightened for four decades — licensing from 1951, state dominance from the 1956 resolution, and MRTP curbs from 1969 — before the 1991 policy dismantled the 'licence raj' almost overnight.

subject: Environment
theme: Environmental Legislation and Events in India

items.label: Wildlife (Protection) Act passed
Project Tiger launched
Forest (Conservation) Act passed
Bhopal Gas Tragedy
National Green Tribunal Act passed

explanation: India's environmental legal framework built up gradually — protection statutes in the 1970s and 80s, an industrial-disaster wake-up call in 1984, and eventually a dedicated judicial body (NGT) in 2010 to fast-track environmental cases.

subject: Environment

items.label: Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment
Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances
Rio Earth Summit adopts the UNFCCC and CBD
Kyoto Protocol sets binding emission targets
Paris Agreement adopted

explanation: Stockholm put environment on the global agenda, Montreal proved treaties could work (on ozone), Rio created the climate and biodiversity conventions, and Kyoto's binding targets eventually gave way to the Paris Agreement's universal pledges.

subject: Environment

items.label: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act
Environment (Protection) Act — the umbrella law
Biological Diversity Act
Forest Rights Act recognises rights of forest dwellers

explanation: Pollution law came medium by medium — water in 1974, air in 1981 — until Bhopal prompted the umbrella Environment Protection Act of 1986; the 2000s added biodiversity governance and, in 2006, statutory rights for forest-dwelling communities.

subject: Environment

items.label: Project Tiger launched
Crocodile Conservation Project begins
Project Elephant launched
Project Snow Leopard launched
Cheetahs reintroduced at Kuno National Park

explanation: Flagship-species programmes began with Project Tiger in 1973 and spread to crocodiles, elephants and snow leopards; the 2022 cheetah translocation from Africa was the world's first intercontinental reintroduction of a large carnivore.

subject: Environment
theme: Milestone COPs of the Climate Convention

items.label: COP1 held at Berlin
COP3 at Kyoto adopts the Kyoto Protocol
COP13 adopts the Bali Action Plan
COP15 at Copenhagen ends without a binding deal
COP21 adopts the Paris Agreement

explanation: The COP sequence tells the negotiation story: Kyoto's top-down binding targets, the Bali roadmap seeking a successor, Copenhagen's collapse — and the pivot to Paris's bottom-up nationally determined contributions in 2015.

subject: Environment
theme: Protected Areas and Wetlands in India

items.label: Hailey (now Corbett) National Park, India's first, created
Ramsar Convention on Wetlands adopted
Chilika and Keoladeo become India's first Ramsar sites
Nilgiri becomes India's first biosphere reserve

explanation: India's protected-area toolkit expanded over half a century: the first national park under colonial rule in 1936, international wetland designations after India joined the Ramsar regime (first sites 1981), and UNESCO-style biosphere reserves from 1986.

subject: Environment

items.label: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer
Montreal Protocol adopted
Montreal Protocol enters into force
Kigali Amendment targets HFCs
India ratifies the Kigali Amendment

explanation: The Vienna framework of 1985 led within two years to the Montreal Protocol's binding phase-outs of CFCs; decades later the Kigali Amendment extended the regime to HFCs — potent greenhouse gases — with India ratifying in 2021.

subject: Environment

items.label: CITES signed to regulate wildlife trade
Convention on Biological Diversity opened at Rio
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety adopted
Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted

explanation: Wildlife-trade control (CITES) came first; the CBD then anchored biodiversity law from 1992, gaining protocols on GMO trade (Cartagena) and genetic-resource benefit sharing (Nagoya) before the 2022 framework set the '30 by 30' targets.

subject: Environment

items.label: Khejarli sacrifice — Bishnois die protecting trees
Chipko movement begins in the Garhwal Himalaya
Appiko movement in the Western Ghats of Karnataka
Narmada Bachao Andolan takes shape

explanation: The Bishnoi sacrifice of 1730 is the movement tradition's origin story; Chipko revived tree-hugging protest in the 1970s Himalaya, Appiko carried it south to Karnataka, and the NBA turned the energy against large dams on the Narmada.

subject: Environment

items.label: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act
National Ambient Air Quality Standards revised (12 pollutants)
BS-IV fuel norms enforced nationwide
National Clean Air Programme launched
India leapfrogs to BS-VI fuel norms

explanation: Regulation accelerated sharply in the late 2010s: after decades under the 1981 Act and the 2009 standards, India rolled out BS-IV nationally in 2017, launched city-level NCAP targets in 2019, and skipped BS-V entirely to enforce BS-VI in 2020.

subject: Environment

items.label: First Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification
Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules notified
CRZ Notification comprehensively revised
Wetlands Rules replaced with a decentralised framework
CRZ Notification eases norms with graded zones

explanation: Both regimes were born under the Environment Protection Act and repeatedly rewritten: CRZ rules issued in 1991 were overhauled in 2011 and relaxed in 2019, while wetland rules moved from central control (2010) to state-led management (2017).

subject: Environment
theme: Institutions and Reports of Global Environmentalism

items.label: UNEP established after Stockholm
Brundtland Report defines sustainable development
IPCC established by UNEP and WMO
IPCC releases its First Assessment Report
UN adopts the Sustainable Development Goals

explanation: UNEP institutionalised the Stockholm agenda; the Brundtland Report's 'sustainable development' framing (1987) and the IPCC's first assessment (1990) built the scientific-political consensus that eventually produced the SDGs in 2015.

subject: Polity

items.label: Constitution of India adopted by the Constituent Assembly
Constitution comes into force
First Amendment Act
42nd Amendment ('Mini Constitution')
73rd and 74th Amendments (Panchayati Raj and Municipalities)

explanation: From adoption to enforcement took two months. The First Amendment quickly addressed land-reform and free-speech tensions; the 42nd Amendment during the Emergency reshaped the Preamble and Centre-State balance; and the 73rd/74th Amendments finally gave local self-government constitutional status.

subject: Polity

items.label: Cabinet Mission arrives in India
Constituent Assembly holds its first sitting
Objectives Resolution adopted
Constitution adopted
Constitution comes into force

explanation: The Cabinet Mission's plan created the Constituent Assembly, which first met on 9 December 1946; Nehru's Objectives Resolution (adopted January 1947) became the Preamble's seed, and the finished Constitution was adopted in November 1949 and enforced on 26 January 1950.

subject: Polity

items.label: First general elections begin
EVMs first used in a Kerala by-election
Voting age lowered from 21 to 18 (61st Amendment)
NOTA option introduced after a Supreme Court ruling
VVPAT deployed at every polling station

explanation: The world's largest electoral exercise has kept upgrading itself — universal adult franchise from the very first election of 1951-52, machines from 1982, a younger electorate from 1989, and voter-verification tools (NOTA, VVPAT) in the 2010s.

subject: Polity

items.label: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommends three-tier panchayats
Ashok Mehta Committee reviews Panchayati Raj
73rd Amendment gives panchayats constitutional status
PESA extends panchayats to Scheduled Areas

explanation: Democratic decentralisation moved from committee reports (Balwant Rai Mehta 1957, Ashok Mehta 1977) to constitutional guarantee with the 73rd Amendment, and PESA then adapted the framework for tribal Scheduled Areas in 1996.

subject: Polity

items.label: Shankari Prasad case upholds Parliament's amending power
Golaknath case bars amending Fundamental Rights
Kesavananda Bharati case propounds the basic structure doctrine
Minerva Mills case strikes down parts of the 42nd Amendment
I. R. Coelho case applies basic structure review to the Ninth Schedule

explanation: The Court swung from deference (Shankari Prasad) to rigidity (Golaknath) before Kesavananda's 1973 compromise: Parliament may amend anything except the Constitution's basic structure — a doctrine reinforced in Minerva Mills and extended to the Ninth Schedule in 2007.

subject: Polity

items.label: Central Public Service Commission set up
Election Commission of India established
First Finance Commission constituted
National Human Rights Commission established
Central Information Commission constituted under the RTI Act

explanation: The merit-based PSC predates independence; the Constitution then created the ECI (25 January 1950 — celebrated as National Voters' Day) and the Finance Commission, while statutory watchdogs for human rights (1993) and information (2005) came much later.

subject: Polity

items.label: First National Emergency proclaimed during the China war
Second National Emergency during the Bangladesh war
Internal Emergency proclaimed on grounds of 'internal disturbance'
Emergency revoked; Janata government takes office
44th Amendment makes Emergency proclamation harder

explanation: India's three national emergencies came in 1962, 1971 and 1975 — the last an internal one that triggered a democratic backlash; the Janata government's 44th Amendment then replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground.

subject: Polity

items.label: Government of India Act transfers power to the Crown
Indian Councils Act adds Indians to legislative councils
Indian Councils Act introduces indirect elections
Morley-Minto reforms introduce separate electorates
Government of India Act provides provincial autonomy

explanation: Each act conceded slightly more representation: nominated Indians in 1861, indirect election in 1892, separate electorates in 1909, and finally the 1935 Act — whose federal and provincial machinery became the working draft for the Indian Constitution.

subject: Polity

items.label: 24th Amendment affirms Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights
52nd Amendment introduces the anti-defection law
86th Amendment makes education a fundamental right
101st Amendment enables the GST
103rd Amendment provides 10% EWS reservation

explanation: These amendments each rewired a different arena — Parliament versus judiciary (24th), party discipline (52nd), social rights (86th), fiscal federalism (101st) and reservation policy (103rd).

subject: Polity

items.label: Maneka Gandhi case widens Article 21's 'procedure established by law'
Vishaka guidelines against workplace sexual harassment
NALSA judgment recognises transgender identity
Puttaswamy judgment declares privacy a fundamental right
Navtej Singh Johar decriminalises consensual same-sex relations

explanation: Maneka Gandhi's expansive reading of Article 21 is the fountainhead: every later case here — Vishaka, NALSA, Puttaswamy, Navtej Johar — built dignity, equality and privacy protections on that foundation.

subject: Polity

items.label: Mandal Commission constituted
V. P. Singh government implements Mandal recommendations
Indra Sawhney judgment caps reservation at 50%
93rd Amendment enables OBC quotas in educational institutions
103rd Amendment adds 10% EWS reservation

explanation: A decade separated the Mandal Commission's creation from its explosive implementation in 1990; Indra Sawhney then set the 50% ceiling and creamy-layer rule, while later amendments extended quotas to education (2005) and economic criteria (2019).

subject: Polity

items.label: Right to Information Act enacted
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act passed
Whistle Blowers Protection Act enacted
First Lokpal of India appointed

explanation: RTI opened government records in 2005; the anti-corruption wave after 2011 produced the Lokpal Act (2013) and whistle-blower protection (2014), though the first Lokpal was appointed only in 2019 — six years after the law.
